newsitem.title: UK: BoE' George demands 1/4 point rate rise in latest.
newsitem.headline: BoE' George demands 1/4 point rate rise in latest.

text.p: Britain's six percent official interest rate needs to be increased by 25 basis points to check building inflation pressures, Bank of England Governor Eddie George said at the March 5 monetary meeting.
"The Bank continues to advise therefore that interest rates be raised now by a 1/4 percent," the minutes quoted George saying.

"The Bank's concern was that, if, on the account of the exchange rate the necessary tightening of policy to moderate the pace of domestic expansion was delayed, then more substantial tightening would eventually become unavoidable," the minutes said.
But Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said not a great deal had changed since the last meeting and the extra information had not justified a change in view.
So he and the Governor remained a quarter percentage point apart on the appropriate level of interest rates.
That reflected a small disagreement about the outlook for inflation one to two years ahead and about the balance of risks.
Clarke decided to leave interest rates unchanged "for the moment."
The Chancellor said in his view: "The upside and downside risks associated with the prospect for inflation two years out were very balanced."
Since the last meeting, the upside risk of unsustainably strong consumer demand had eased somewhat and the exchange rate had strengthened further, he said.
During the discussion, both sides agreed that if the exchange rate remained very high this would have a deflationary effect.
"But it's main effect on inflation would be relatively short-term and temporary," the minutes said.

George said since the previous meeting both the monetary data and activity indicators had perked up, confirming the central bank's view that the apparent softening at the end of last year, was in fact erratic.

The persistence of rapid monetary growth and above-trend growth of consumer demand and overall output represented "a developing threat to the inflation target as we move through next year," George said.
The Bank expects Britain's targeted measure of inflation, RPIX, to come down during the coming months as the effects of sterling's appreciation and lower producer prices work their way through.
"Though the speed and extent of this pass through was necessarily uncertain," George said.
He expected RPIX to fall below the 2.5 percent target by the end of this year. But the prospects for inflation in 1998 and beyond were more uncertain.
